# Uniform lattice sampling and a partial-continuum depth limit

**Status: proved elementary discrepancy and fixed-body limit statements;
independent audit pending.** These statements track all halfspaces,
including cuts carrying lattice-fiber boundary mass. The partial limit
does not prove OC for the remaining discrete variables. A conditional
induction implication is stated as conditional, not as a resolution.

## 1. A uniform discrepancy for every bounded convex set

Let r>=1, s>=0, m=r+s, and write R^m=R^r times R^s. Let L+t be a
full-rank lattice coset in R^r with a measurable fundamental cell P
centered at zero, whose translates tile up to null sets and satisfy
P subset [-delta,delta]^r. Write v_L for its covolume. For every compact
convex Q subset [-R,R]^m, including empty or lower-dimensional Q, put

    mu_L(Q)=v_L sum_(lambda in L+t) vol_s(Q_lambda).

Here vol_0 is counting measure on the singleton R^0. Then

    |mu_L(Q)-vol_m(Q)|
        <= epsilon(r,s,R,delta)
         :=2r delta (2R+2delta)^(m-1).                     (1)

To prove this, form the measurable union

    U=union_(lambda in L+t) ((lambda+P) times Q_lambda).

The union's volume is mu_L(Q), by disjointness of the base cells up to
null sets and Fubini. With E=[-delta,delta]^r times {0}, one has

    Q minus E subset U subset Q plus E,                   (2)

where the lower inclusion is understood up to a null base cylinder,
and minus denotes Minkowski erosion {x:x+E subset Q}. The upper
inclusion follows by moving the base from lambda to its cell point.
For the lower inclusion choose the cell containing a given base: its
sample base differs in each coordinate by at most delta, so the sampled
point remains in Q. A choice on cell boundaries is immaterial to volume.

For any convex compact A and a coordinate unit vector e_i, Fubini along
that coordinate gives the exact identity

    vol_m(A+[-delta,delta]e_i)-vol_m(A)
        =2delta vol_(m-1)(projection_(e_i-perp) A).         (3)

Each nonempty line section is an interval, including a possible point;
adding the segment increases its length by 2delta. The identity also
holds for lower-dimensional A. Similarly, erosion by that segment
removes length min(2delta,ell) from a line section of length ell. Hence

    vol_m(A)-vol_m(A minus [-delta,delta]e_i)
        <=2delta vol_(m-1)(projection_(e_i-perp) A).        (4)

Successively dilating in the first r coordinate directions keeps the
sets inside [-R-delta,R+delta]^m, so each projection volume in (3) is
at most (2R+2delta)^(m-1). Successive erosions stay inside [-R,R]^m,
and (4) is bounded by 2delta(2R)^(m-1) at each step. Erosion by a sum
of segments equals successive erosion, directly from its definition.
Summing these r estimates and applying (2) proves (1).

When m=1, vol_0 of a nonempty projection is one. The same interval
argument gives (3)--(4), including empty sets. No differentiability,
Riemann integrability of a sampled density, or boundary-null assertion
about mu_L is required. In particular (1) applies with exactly the same
constant to EVERY Q=K intersect H when K subset [-R,R]^m is convex and
H is an arbitrary closed halfspace.

One may use centered half-open parallelepipeds as P. Alternatively a
Voronoi cell, with a measurable assignment of its null boundaries, fits
inside the coordinate cube whenever the lattice covering radius is at
most delta. The estimates only use the stated tiling and containment.

## 2. Partial sampling with fixed remaining integer bases

Write the full space as R^k times R^r times R^s, with k>=0,r>=1,s>=0.
Let K be a FIXED compact convex body contained in [-R,R]^(k+r+s).
Assume the measure

    nu(A)=sum_(j in Z^k) vol_(r+s)({x:(j,x) in K intersect A})

has total mass M>0. Thus the coarse mixed set has positive full
(r+s)-dimensional fiber measure. Let L_l+t_l be full-rank lattice
cosets in R^r with cells as above, delta_l ->0, and define

    mu_l(A)=v_(L_l) sum_(j in Z^k, lambda in L_l+t_l)
                  vol_s({x:(j,lambda,x) in K intersect A}).

There are at most J=(2 floor(R)+1)^k possible j (with J=1 if k=0).
Applying (1) to each convex coarse fiber cut gives

    sup_(closed halfspaces H) |mu_l(H)-nu(H)| <= J epsilon_l,
    |mu_l(total)-M| <= J epsilon_l,                        (5)

where epsilon_l=epsilon(r,s,R,delta_l). Both statements include coarse
fibers of zero (r+s)-volume: their fine-grid samples are bounded by the
same discrepancy, rather than being silently discarded. In particular
mu_l(total)>0 for all sufficiently large l. After normalization, (5)
implies a quantity e_l ->0 such that

    sup_H |mu_l(H)/mu_l(total)-nu(H)/M| <= e_l.              (6)

For example e_l=2J epsilon_l/(M-J epsilon_l) works once its denominator
is positive. It follows immediately that the two normalized depth
functions, evaluated at any SAME ambient point, differ by at most e_l.
This is halfspace discrepancy, not total-variation convergence between
the singular grid measure and the continuum measure.

## 3. Recovery of a single feasible center and convergence of maximal depth

Let S_c=K intersect (Z^k times R^(r+s)), and
S_l=K intersect (Z^k times (L_l+t_l) times R^s). Depths below use nu/M
and mu_l/mu_l(total) respectively. Then

    lim_l sup_(y in S_l) depth_(mu_l)(y)
         = sup_(y in S_c) depth_nu(y).                     (7)

The upper bound follows from S_l subset S_c and (6). To prove the
lower bound, fix a point y=(j,z) in S_c of strictly positive coarse
depth. Let P_+ be the finite set of bases of positive-volume coarse
fibers. Necessarily j belongs to conv(P_+): otherwise strict separation
in base space yields a through-y closed halfspace having nu-mass zero.
Since j is a convex combination of bases in P_+, convexity implies its
own fiber K_j has full dimension r+s. Indeed the corresponding Minkowski
combination of their fibers lies in K_j, and any positive-weight
full-dimensional summand already makes that combination full dimensional.

Depth is Lipschitz as a function of z inside a fixed j-fiber, with a
finite uniform constant. For a nonzero continuous normal, normalize its
(r+s)-part to length one; translating the point by h changes every
fiber's threshold by at most |h|. A section of any coarse fiber inside
the Euclidean ball of radius R sqrt(r+s) has (r+s-1)-volume at most
(2R sqrt(r+s))^(r+s-1). Fubini bounds each lost slab by this number
times |h|, uniformly in the integer coefficients, which may be arbitrarily
large. Sum over at most J positive fibers and divide by M. For a purely
integer normal the through-point halfspace is unchanged by h. Taking
the infimum over all normals preserves the Lipschitz estimate. Coarse
zero-volume fibers do not affect nu; r+s>=1 avoids an atomic continuous
section exception.

Choose z' in int(K_j) arbitrarily close to z, losing arbitrarily little
coarse depth, and keep this point fixed. The translates of P cover almost
every base point, so the larger closed cubes
lambda+[-delta_l,delta_l]^r cover EVERY base point: their union is locally
finite and therefore closed, while its complement is both open and null.
Round only the first r coordinates to a sample base lambda_l whose closed
cube contains those coordinates. The Euclidean displacement is at most
sqrt(r) delta_l. This selection does not require membership in a
fundamental cell at one of its omitted boundary points.
Leave the last s coordinates unchanged. Since z' is an interior point,
the rounded point y_l belongs to K_j for all large l, hence y_l in S_l.
Its coarse depth converges to that of (j,z') by the Lipschitz estimate,
and (6) transfers this to its fine depth. Finally let z' approach z and
let y range over arbitrarily near-maximal positive-depth coarse points.

There is at least one positive-depth coarse point: any positive-volume
fiber has an interior ordinary centroid and contributes a positive
fraction to every containing ambient cap. Thus the argument indeed
approaches the supremum. This proves (7) with a deterministic feasible
sequence and no selection by expectation. Existence of a maximizing
point is unnecessary for (7); approximate maximizers suffice.

## 4. What the limit would give to an induction

Set n=k+r, d=s. If the exact OC theorem is available for (k,s+r), then
the right side of (7) is at least 2^-k Gamma_(s+r). Therefore the fine
mixed problem eventually has depth at least 2^(-k-r) Gamma_s whenever

    2^-k Gamma_(s+r) > 2^(-k-r) Gamma_s.                   (8)

This strict inequality holds except when r=1 and s=0: if s>=1,
Gamma_s<=1/2 while Gamma_(s+r)>1/e>1/4, and 2^r>=2; if s=0,r>=2,
Gamma_r>1/e>1/4>=2^-r. The exceptional equality is
Gamma_1=Gamma_0/2=1/2. All Gamma indices here have their usual convention
Gamma_0=1. The simple numerical facts can also be obtained directly from
the monotonicity of (m/(m+1))^m and its limit 1/e.

For k=0 the needed coarse theorem is classical continuous Grunbaum,
so (7) gives an unconditional eventual bound in this fixed-body dense
lattice regime in the strict cases above. The exceptional k=0,r=1,s=0
case instead follows directly from the discrete median of the finite
nonempty arithmetic progression; (7) alone would not imply its exact
finite-grid bound. For k>0 this paragraph is an INDUCTION IMPLICATION;
it does not invoke the unproved general OC as if already established.

The body K is fixed and the full coarse mixed volume is positive. The
proof makes no claim that an arbitrary bad sequence of convex bodies
can be put into this form, that boundary coarse fibers persist under
varying-body Hausdorff limits, or that a general lattice automatically
splits into the fixed and dense factors used here. Those are separate
issues. In particular (7) is not a compactification of every OC instance.

## 5. An extension with explicitly converging coarse fibers

Here is a valid varying-body extension, with its additional hypotheses
stated rather than inferred from ambient Hausdorff convergence. Suppose
K_l are convex bodies inside the same bounded box and have the SAME
finite set P of nonempty coarse integer fibers. Write these compact
convex fibers as Q_(l,j) subset R^(r+s), j in P. Suppose

    Q_(l,j) -> Q_j in Hausdorff distance for every j in P,
    M_*=sum_(j in P) vol_(r+s)(Q_j)>0.                    (9)

Use the fine lattice cosets and delta_l ->0 as before. Define nu_* as
the sum of full (r+s)-volume on the Q_j and S_* as their lifted union.
Then the maximal normalized fine depth converges to the maximal
normalized depth of nu_* with centers in S_*.

Indeed uniform measures of the convex fibers converge in total variation
as unnormalized measures. A full-dimensional limiting fiber gives
almost-everywhere indicator convergence off its null boundary. A
lower-dimensional limiting fiber has volume tending to zero, so the L1
norm of its indicator tends to zero. Summing finitely many fibers proves
total-variation convergence of their coarse measures. Combining it with
the uniform estimate (5) gives uniform normalized halfspace discrepancy
between the fine measures and nu_*, tending to zero.

The limiting fibers are convex-compatible. For any convex combination
of bases j_i in P whose mean is j in P, approximate points of Q_(j_i)
by points of Q_(l,j_i), apply convexity in K_l, and pass to the limit
in Q_(l,j). This gives sum t_i Q_(j_i) subset Q_j. Also
P=conv(P) intersect Z^k, since every integer base in conv(P) has a
nonempty fiber in each K_l. Therefore D=conv(union_j {j} times Q_j)
has exactly the coarse integer fibers Q_j and no others.

For the upper bound on maximal fine depth, choose approximate maximizing
fine points along a subsequence realizing the limsup. Boundedness and
finiteness of P give a further subsequence with fixed coarse base j
and continuous coordinates converging to a point z in Q_j. The normalized
nu_* depth is Lipschitz along every fixed coarse base by the same slab
argument as Section 3, whether or not that base has positive own volume.
Uniform halfspace discrepancy and this continuity bound the limsup by
the maximal depth on S_*.

For the lower bound, a positive-depth point of S_* has a full-dimensional
own fiber, by the base-hull and compatibility argument from Section 3.
Approximate it inside that fiber by z'. Hausdorff convergence to this
full-dimensional fiber puts a fixed neighborhood of z' in Q_(l,j) for
all large l. Rounding only its fine-lattice coordinates therefore gives
feasible points in K_l. The same uniform discrepancy and fixed-base
Lipschitz estimate recover their depths. This proves the claimed limit.

For clarity, S_* can be realized by an actual full-dimensional ambient
convex body, despite possible loss of ambient dimension in D. If P spans
R^k, one full (r+s)-fiber together with the spanning bases makes D full
dimensional. Otherwise A=aff(P) is proper. The compact polytope conv(P)
has positive distance from all integer points outside P; choose a
smaller positive neighborhood radius. Select a small full-dimensional
ambient ball whose base projection lies in that neighborhood of
conv(P) and strictly to one side of an affine hyperplane containing A.
Its convex hull with D is full dimensional. Its projection is still in
the chosen neighborhood and hence has no integer bases outside P.
At bases in P, the separating affine functional is zero, so no positive
weight from the added ball can enter their fibers. All Q_j are therefore
preserved EXACTLY. For k=0, positive M_* already makes D full dimensional.

This extension permits the induction implication of Section 4 whenever
the hypotheses (9) and the stated fixed-base/dense-lattice decomposition
have actually been established. It does not supply that decomposition
for arbitrary moving lattices, nor handle the case M_*=0. The latter
would require a different normalization or an intrinsic-dimensional
analysis, not cancellation of a vanishing total mass.
